subject: Computer Networking
title: Clients and Servers
description: Learn Clients and Servers in one minute.

hook.text: You type a URL. A page appears. Behind the scenes, two machines just had a conversation.

buildup.text: Your device is the client — it asks for things. The server is a remote computer that has what you need.

discovery.text: Clients send requests. Servers send responses. Every website, app, and API follows this pattern.

twist.text: A single server can talk to millions of clients at once. That's why big sites need massive infrastructure.

climax.text: Even your phone acts as a server sometimes — sharing files or hosting a hotspot for other devices.

punchline.text: Client asks, server answers. The internet in two words.

quiz.question: In the client-server model, what does the client do?
options: Sends requests for data or services
Stores all the website's files permanently
Manages the physical cables of the internet

details.summary: In the client-server model, clients request services and servers provide them. Your browser is a client that requests web pages from servers. This model organizes most internet communication, though peer-to-peer networks offer an alternative where every device is both client and server.
details.whyItMatters: The client-server model is the foundation of web architecture. Understanding it explains how browsers, apps, and APIs interact with remote systems.
takeaways: Clients request resources; servers respond with them
Most internet services use the client-server model
Peer-to-peer is an alternative where all nodes are equal

faq.question: Can a device be both a client and a server?
faq.answer: Yes. A device running a web server can serve pages to others while its browser acts as a client to other servers. In peer-to-peer networks like BitTorrent, every device simultaneously uploads and downloads, acting as both client and server.

faq.question: Why is the client-server model dominant over peer-to-peer?
faq.answer: Centralized servers are easier to secure, manage, and scale. They provide consistent availability and performance. Peer-to-peer lacks central control, making it harder to ensure reliability. However, P2P excels at distributing large files efficiently.
